overview: AES is a global power generation and utility holding company, incorporated in 1981 and headquartered in Arlington, Virginia, operating a diversified portfolio of approximately 34,740 MW of generation plus two U.S. regulated utilities (AES Indiana and AES Ohio) and four distribution utilities in El Salvador serving 2.7 million customers. The company is organized into four technology-based strategic business units (SBUs) -- Renewables, Utilities, Energy Infrastructure, and New Energy Technologies -- with operations spanning the U.S. and Latin America/Caribbean (Chile, Colombia, Panama, Dominican Republic, Argentina, Mexico, Puerto Rico) plus smaller positions in Vietnam, Bulgaria, Jordan, and the Netherlands. On March 1, 2026, AES agreed to be acquired for $15.00/share in cash by Horizon Parent, L.P., a consortium led by Global Infrastructure Partners (a BlackRock company) and EQT, with CalPERS and the Qatar Investment Authority also participating; the deal (~$10.7B equity value / ~$33.4B enterprise value) has been approved by shareholders and most regulators and is expected to close late 2026 or early 2027.

business_model.summary: AES earns the large majority of its earnings from long-term contracted generation (PPAs with utilities, industrials, mining companies, and increasingly data-center hyperscalers) and from rate-regulated utility returns in Indiana and Ohio, supplemented by shorter-term/merchant power sales and U.S. renewable tax credit monetization. Reported net income to AES shareholders is heavily diluted by noncontrolling interests and redeemable stock of subsidiaries (tax equity investors, minority JV partners such as CDPQ in AES Ohio/Indiana, and project-level partners), which absorbed $748 million of net losses in 2025 alone.

revenue_streams.name: Energy Infrastructure SBU (gas/LNG/coal/pet coke/oil generation, 9 countries)
Utilities SBU (AES Indiana, AES Ohio, AES El Salvador)
New Energy Technologies (Fluence, Maximo, other investments)

business_model.customer_type: B2B/wholesale -- regulated utility ratepayers (residential/commercial/industrial via AES Indiana, AES Ohio, El Salvador distribution), corporate/hyperscaler offtakers under long-term PPAs (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Apple, Meta, Constellation, various RTO/ISO markets), and mining/industrial customers in Chile, Colombia, and Panama
business_model.geographic_mix: United States (utilities + renewables growth platform + Southland CA conventional generation), Chile/Colombia/Panama/Dominican Republic/Argentina/Mexico/Puerto Rico (Latin America generation and utilities), plus smaller legacy positions in Vietnam, Bulgaria, Jordan, and the Netherlands

competitive_position.market_position: Mid-sized diversified power producer; consistently rated by Bloomberg New Energy Finance as one of the top two largest global sellers of renewable power to corporate customers; leading U.S. renewables growth platform (AES Clean Energy) with a 46 GW development pipeline; small regulated utilities (AES Indiana ~533,000 customers, AES Ohio ~541,000 customers) that are among the fastest-growing U.S. utility rate bases; roughly 5-16% market share in several of its smaller Latin American/Caribbean markets (Chile ~6%, Colombia ~5%, Panama ~16%, Argentina ~3%)

moat_factors.description: Majority of generation is sold under medium/long-term PPAs that pass through fuel costs and provide capacity payments covering fixed costs and a return on capital, insulating cash flow from short-term price swings
AES Indiana and AES Ohio hold exclusive service-territory rights with regulator-approved rate-base returns, though subject to periodic rate case risk

Deep, repeat relationships with large technology companies (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Apple) for data-center power, built on a track record of on-time, on-budget delivery; 12 GW of backlog with signed PPAs
46 GW U.S. renewables development pipeline and global development/EPC capabilities provide a sizable growth runway, though execution-dependent

moat_factors.factor: Local market barriers in some LatAm utilities
moat_factors.description: El Salvador distribution utilities face limited competition due to regulatory barriers to entry

weaknesses: No durable cost or technology advantage versus larger, better-capitalized peers (NextEra, Brookfield) in renewables development
Complex, non-recourse project-debt and tax-equity/NCI structure dilutes AES shareholders' share of consolidated earnings and complicates valuation
Geographically fragmented portfolio across many small countries increases operational and political complexity relative to scale
History of a material weakness in internal controls (AES Brasil disposition/impairment, remediated as of year-end 2025) signaling elevated accounting/financial-reporting risk
Heavy reliance on continued access to capital markets (non-recourse and recourse debt) to fund growth given limited free cash flow after growth capex

growth_drivers: 12.0 GW signed-contract renewables backlog (5.7 GW under construction) as of year-end 2025, with 4.0 GW of new long-term PPAs signed/awarded in 2025 alone

Data-center/AI power demand: ~12 GW signed with data-center customers (~9 GW direct hyperscaler PPAs), including a landmark February 2026 20-year co-located PPA with Google in Texas, plus relationships with Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, Meta, and others

U.S. utility rate-base growth: AES Indiana and AES Ohio are projecting double-digit rate-base growth through 2027, including a $4.2 billion AES Indiana capital program (2026-2028) and new large-load/data-center infrastructure investment (e.g., the Monrovia, Indiana data-center campus project approved by the IURC in October 2026)
46 GW U.S. renewables development pipeline (AES Clean Energy) positioned to capture generative-AI-driven electricity demand growth
Monetization of U.S. renewable tax credits (ITC/PTC, including IRA transferability provisions) -- $1.5 billion recognized in 2025 -- though curtailed somewhat by the 2025 tax act (H.R. 1)
Portfolio rationalization / asset sales (e.g., AGIC minority stake sale for $450 million in Q1 2025, Dominican Republic Renewables sell-down) recycling capital into higher-return growth
Pending take-private transaction ($15.00/share cash, GIP/EQT-led consortium) would resolve standalone balance-sheet and dividend-sustainability concerns and inject private capital for growth

business.risk: Heavy exposure to developing-country operating risk
business.description: Significant revenue from Chile, Colombia, Panama, Dominican Republic, Argentina, Mexico, and El Salvador exposes AES to political instability, currency controls, expropriation risk, and counterparty non-performance
PREPA remains in Title III bankruptcy; AES Ilumina's $18 million non-recourse debt is in technical default; litigation over PREPA's net revenues continues with hearings into late 2026
U.S. interconnection queues average over four years; projects face permitting, siting, supply-chain, and community-opposition risk before reaching construction-ready status
Non-contracted/merchant generation and hydro-dependent plants (Panama, Colombia, Chile) are exposed to spot power prices, fuel costs, and weather/hydrological variability

financial.risk: High consolidated leverage via non-recourse and recourse debt
financial.description: As of September 30, 2026, AES carried $26 billion of non-recourse debt and $6.4 billion of recourse debt ($32.7 billion gross total), with $10.4 billion accruing interest at variable rates

Net losses attributable to NCI and redeemable stock of subsidiaries were $748 million in 2025 (vs. net income to AES shareholders of $910 million), reflecting large allocations to tax-equity investors and minority partners (CDPQ in AES Ohio/Indiana, GIP in Chile renewables, TotalEnergies in Puerto Rico) that complicate earnings interpretation

Argentine peso devaluation risk and Chilean/Colombian peso swings drove a $79 million net foreign-currency transaction loss in 2025; AES generally matches revenue/debt currency but residual exposure remains
AES's board chairman stated that without the pending transaction, AES would likely need to reduce or eliminate its dividend and/or issue substantial new equity to address its capital structure

regulatory.description: Though shareholder approval, HSR, CFIUS, EU, Ohio PUCO, and New York PSC clearances have been obtained, the deal still requires remaining regulatory approvals (e.g., FERC) and customary closing conditions; the outside date is June 1, 2027 (with possible extensions), and merger-related shareholder litigation is ongoing
The 2025 tax act (H.R. 1) curtailed IRA-era renewable tax incentives; AES believes its backlog is largely safe-harbored but acknowledges potential adverse impact on future PPAs and project economics

AES Ohio's Three-Year Rate Plan and AES Indiana's 2026 Base Rate Order both face pending appeals/reconsideration petitions (OUCC, CAC) that could affect approved returns on equity and recovery mechanisms

Numerous evolving EPA rules on coal combustion residuals, GHG emissions, cooling water intake, and MATS create compliance-cost uncertainty, though recent federal deregulatory actions have been net favorable

macro.description: High leverage and continued reliance on debt markets to fund renewables/utility capex make AES sensitive to borrowing costs and refinancing conditions
Argentine peso deterioration risk, with potential for a devaluation event similar to 2018/2019/2023

macro.risk: Global supply chain and tariff risk for renewables equipment
macro.description: Tariffs/duties on imported solar cells, modules, batteries, and wind components could raise project costs or delay the U.S. renewables buildout

macro_factors.industry_outlook: U.S. power demand growth is re-accelerating after two decades of flatness, driven by data centers/generative AI and electrification/reshoring of manufacturing, benefiting both AES's regulated utilities (rate-base growth) and its contracted renewables/storage platform; Latin American power markets offer steady but currency- and hydrology-exposed growth
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate -- utility and long-term-PPA cash flows are relatively defensive, but merchant/short-term generation, Latin American spot markets, and renewables development activity are more cyclical and commodity/weather sensitive
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High -- large non-recourse and recourse debt load, continued capital-intensive growth, and reliance on tax-equity/NCI financing structures make AES's cost of capital and project economics sensitive to rates
key_input_costs: Solar modules and wind turbine equipment

recent_developments.event: AES agreed to be acquired for $15.00/share in cash (~$10.7B equity value, ~$33.4B enterprise value) by Horizon Parent, L.P., a consortium led by Global Infrastructure Partners (BlackRock) and EQT Infrastructure VI, with CalPERS and Qatar Investment Authority also participating
AES stockholders approved the merger at a special meeting (June 26, 2026); HSR waiting period expired June 22, 2026
Ohio PUCO approved the merger application (September 17, 2026); subject to an OCC motion for rehearing seeking investment-grade/ring-fencing conditions

European Commission unconditionally approved the merger (October 15, 2026); New York PSC ruled no further review required (October 19, 2026); IURC approved AES Indiana's plan to serve the Monrovia, Indiana data-center campus (October 7, 2026)
AES and Google signed 20-year PPAs for power co-located with a new Google data center in Wilbarger County, Texas

AES Indiana and AES Ohio pursued multi-year rate settlements (2026 Base Rate Order at AES Indiana; Three-Year Rate Plan settlement at AES Ohio) amid Ohio's House Bill 15 reform eliminating prior ESP riders
Management concluded remediation of the previously disclosed material weakness in internal controls (tied to the 2024 AES Brasil disposition/impairment accounting) as of December 31, 2025

DPL (AES Ohio's parent) sold an approximate 30% indirect equity interest in AES Ohio to a CDPQ (La Caisse) subsidiary for ~$544 million; AES also sold a minority interest in its captive insurer AGIC for $450 million, achieving its full-year 2025 asset-sale target of $400-500 million

items.notes: Following the March 2026 merger agreement, AES has not issued updated standalone Adjusted EPS, Adjusted EBITDA, or capex guidance comparable to pre-deal annual guidance; forward-looking disclosure now centers on merger-closing conditions and timing rather than operating targets

items.target: 12.0 GW signed backlog (5.7 GW under construction) at FYE2025; 46 GW U.S. development pipeline
items.notes: Backlog grew from 2025 signings of 4.0 GW of new long-term PPAs; majority of backlog expected online through 2029
Includes generation conversion (Petersburg coal-to-gas), TDSIC investment, and new Monrovia data-center-related infrastructure
Contingent on successful regulatory outcomes in pending Three-Year Rate Plan proceeding
Most major regulatory approvals obtained (HSR, CFIUS, EU, Ohio PUCO, NY PSC, shareholder vote); remaining approvals and customary closing conditions outstanding as of the Q3 2026 10-Q

guidance.management_commentary: Management's forward-looking discussion in the Q3 2026 10-Q is dominated by merger-related risk factors (completion risk, litigation, restrictions on business activity pending close, financing/rating-agency considerations) rather than traditional operating guidance. The AES board chairman has stated that absent the Transaction, AES would likely need a plan involving dividend reduction/elimination and/or substantial new equity issuance, underscoring the capital-structure pressure that motivated the sale.

bull_case: Pending $15.00/share all-cash acquisition by a well-capitalized GIP/EQT-led consortium provides a defined, de-risked exit value for shareholders, with most major regulatory approvals already obtained as of November 2026

Large, de-risked renewables backlog (12.0 GW signed, much of it with investment-grade hyperscaler counterparties) and a 46 GW U.S. development pipeline position AES to capture outsized data-center/AI power demand growth

AES Indiana and AES Ohio are among the fastest rate-base-growth utilities in the U.S., with multi-year rate settlements and new large-load (data center) investment opportunities layered on top of base capital plans

Portfolio simplification (exit from Brazil, reduced Chilean coal exposure, AGIC/AES Ohio minority sell-downs) has focused the company on higher-growth, better-returning businesses and improved 2025 Adjusted EBITDA
Deal structure (private infrastructure capital) could relieve the standalone dividend/equity-issuance pressure management had flagged as likely absent a transaction
bear_case: As a pending acquisition target, AES's upside is effectively capped near the $15.00/share deal price, with the stock behaving as a merger-arbitrage instrument rather than a standalone growth equity; deal-break risk (regulatory, financing, litigation) is the key tail risk

Standalone fundamentals show real stress absent the deal: management itself indicated a need for dividend cuts and/or dilutive equity issuance without the transaction, reflecting a stretched capital structure

High leverage ($32.7 billion gross debt) combined with large noncontrolling-interest/tax-equity allocations make GAAP net income to AES shareholders volatile and difficult to forecast ($910 million in 2025, down 46% from 2024)

Reduction of U.S. renewable tax incentives under the 2025 tax act, elevated interconnection queue times, and tariffs on solar/wind/storage equipment could slow the renewables buildout that is the core growth driver

Significant exposure to Latin American political, currency, and counterparty risk (Argentina peso devaluation risk, Puerto Rico/PREPA bankruptcy, Chilean/Colombian regulatory/hydrology variability) adds volatility that a pure-play U.S. utility would not face
Prior material weakness in internal controls (AES Brasil disposition accounting, remediated year-end 2025) signals elevated financial-reporting risk that investors should continue to monitor
